overview:
Tattvārthasūtra (often written as Tattvarthasutra or Tattvartha Sutra) is one of the most important and widely respected philosophical texts of Jainism. Composed in Sanskrit in aphoristic sūtra style, it presents a systematic summary of Jain doctrine in approximately 350 concise statements (sūtras) arranged in ten chapters. Traditionally attributed to Ācārya Umāsvāti (also known as Umāsvāmi), it is generally dated between the 2nd and 5th centuries CE, a period when many Indian philosophical schools were casting their teachings into brief, memorisable sūtra form. In Jain tradition it is also known as Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra ("Sūtra on the attainment of the meaning of the real principles") and Mokṣa-śāstra ("Treatise on liberation"), indicating both its doctrinal breadth and its soteriological focus.

The title itself is programmatic: "tattva" refers to the fundamental realities or principles, "artha" to their meaning or nature, and "sūtra" to the terse aphoristic form. The work therefore aims to expound the true nature of reality in a highly compressed style. It is regarded as the first major Jain text composed in Sanskrit, marking a transition from earlier Prakrit scriptures to a language that had become the medium of elite philosophical discourse. Because it is accepted as authoritative by both major Jain sects—Digambara and Śvetāmbara—as well as by smaller traditions, it occupies a unique position as a cross-sectarian standard of Jain philosophy.

Structurally, Tattvārthasūtra is divided into ten chapters that move from epistemology and ontology to cosmology, ethics, and the detailed doctrine of karma. The first chapter treats faith and knowledge, outlining different kinds of cognition and the criteria for valid knowledge. Subsequent chapters discuss the nature and classifications of living beings (jīva), the structure of the lower and middle worlds, celestial beings, and the non-living categories (ajīva) such as matter (pudgala), motion (dharma), rest (adharma), space (ākāśa), and time (kāla). The later chapters focus on the influx (āsrava), bondage (bandha), stoppage (saṃvara), and shedding (nirjarā) of karma, culminating in the description of liberation (mokṣa). Within this framework, the text presents the famous seven or nine tattvas (fundamental principles) and integrates them into a coherent path of spiritual progress.

The opening sūtra, "samyag-darśana-jñāna-cāritrāṇi mokṣa-mārgaḥ" (Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct constitute the path to liberation), sets the tone for the entire work. It defines the three jewels (ratnatraya) that together form the mokṣa-mārga, the path leading the soul out of saṃsāra. Throughout the text, doctrinal exposition is closely tied to practical implications: classifications of beings are related to ethical responsibility, and detailed analyses of karmic processes are meant to guide the aspirant in restraining harmful activities and cultivating virtues such as ahiṃsā (non-violence), satya (truthfulness), asteya (non-stealing), brahmacarya (chastity), and aparigraha (non-possessiveness).

Historically, Tattvārthasūtra has attracted a large number of commentaries in Sanskrit and various regional languages, beginning from at least the 5th century CE. These commentaries belong to different sectarian lineages and often debate issues of interpretation, authorship, and doctrinal emphasis. Śvetāmbara tradition generally refers to the author as Umāsvāti and preserves a commentary known as Tattvārthabhāṣya, while Digambara scholars also accept Umāsvāmi but sometimes emphasise different textual recensions and interpretive frameworks. Modern scholarship notes that the text likely predates the fully crystallised division between sects, which helps explain its universal acceptance. At the same time, there are minor variations in chapter divisions and sūtra counts (some recensions list around 344 sūtras, others up to 357), and commentators occasionally disagree on the precise meaning of particular aphorisms.

One of the most famous lines from Tattvārthasūtra is "parasparopagraho jīvanam" ("Living beings are mutually supportive"), which has been adopted as the official motto of Jainism. This aphorism encapsulates the Jain vision of an interconnected universe in which all souls are bound in relationships of mutual dependence and responsibility. It is frequently cited in discussions of Jain ethics, ecology, and non-violence, and modern interpreters often draw on it to articulate Jain contributions to contemporary debates on environmentalism and inter-species ethics.

In the broader landscape of Indian philosophy, Tattvārthasūtra is often compared to texts such as the Brahma-sūtra of Vedānta or Patañjali’s Yoga-sūtra, in the sense that it offers a compact, authoritative formulation of a complex doctrinal system. For Jain communities, it functions as a doctrinal handbook, a text for memorisation and recitation, and a basis for advanced scholastic study. It is regularly read during festivals and in temple settings, and its sūtras are used as starting points for sermons and discourses. While not part of the Śvetāmbara canonical Āgamas, it is nonetheless treated as a highly authoritative synthesis of Jain teaching, bridging scriptural tradition, philosophical reflection, and practical guidance on the path to liberation.

Modern academic studies of Tattvārthasūtra examine its language, structure, and doctrinal content in relation to earlier Jain scriptures and later commentarial traditions. Scholars analyse its treatment of key concepts such as anekāntavāda (the doctrine of non-one-sidedness), the classification of karmas, and the stages of spiritual development (gunasthāna), noting both what is explicitly stated in the sūtras and what is elaborated only in later commentaries. There is ongoing discussion about the exact dating of the text, the historical identity of Umāsvāti, and the relationship between Tattvārthasūtra and other Jain works such as the Digambara Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama or the Śvetāmbara Āgamas. Despite these scholarly debates, the text’s central role as a concise, cross-sectarian exposition of Jain philosophy remains uncontested.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (Tattvarthasutra, Tattvartha-adhigama-sūtra, Mokṣa-śāstra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti (Umāsvāmi)
primary_sources.translation:
“Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct constitute the path to liberation.”
“Living beings are mutually supportive (the function of living beings is to help one another).”
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārthasūtra is a Sanskrit Jain philosophical text composed in aphoristic style, generally dated between the 2nd and 5th centuries CE and attributed to Ācārya Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi. It consists of roughly 350 sūtras in ten chapters, covering knowledge, the nature of living and non-living entities, cosmology, karma theory, ethical vows, and liberation. The opening sūtra defines the three jewels (ratnatraya)—right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct—as the path to mokṣa, framing the entire work as a guide to liberation. The famous sūtra “parasparopagraho jīvanam” has been adopted as the official motto of Jainism and is widely cited in both traditional and modern contexts to express the Jain view of mutual interdependence among living beings. Different recensions of the text show minor variations in sūtra count and wording, and sectarian commentaries sometimes interpret key terms differently, but both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions accept the text’s authority and regard it as a foundational summary of Jain doctrine.

misconceptions.myth: Tattvārthasūtra belongs exclusively to either the Digambara or the Śvetāmbara sect and reflects only that sect’s doctrines.
misconceptions.reality: While later sectarian traditions have claimed the author Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi for their own lineage and produced distinct commentaries, the text itself predates the fully crystallised division between major Jain sects and is accepted as authoritative by both Digambaras and Śvetāmbaras. Its cross-sectarian status is one of its defining features, and doctrinal differences arise more in commentarial interpretation than in the sūtras themselves.

misconceptions.myth: Tattvārthasūtra is simply a devotional scripture and does not engage in rigorous philosophical analysis.
misconceptions.reality: Although it is revered and recited in devotional contexts, Tattvārthasūtra is primarily a philosophical and doctrinal treatise. It systematically discusses epistemology, ontology, cosmology, ethics, and detailed karma theory in a highly condensed form. Later commentaries expand its arguments and show that the sūtras presuppose sophisticated debates about valid cognition, the classification of realities, and the mechanics of karmic bondage and liberation.

misconceptions.myth: The famous motto “parasparopagraho jīvanam” means only that humans should help each other and has no broader doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain interpretation, “parasparopagraho jīvanam” refers to the mutual support and interdependence of all living beings, not just humans. It is grounded in the broader Jain cosmology and ethics, which recognise countless forms of life and emphasise non-violence and responsibility toward all of them. The sūtra is therefore a concise expression of Jain metaphysics and ethics, not merely a general moral slogan.

misconceptions.myth: Because Tattvārthasūtra is short and aphoristic, it can be fully understood without reference to commentaries or broader Jain scriptural tradition.
misconceptions.reality: The brevity of the sūtras is intentional and presupposes prior knowledge of Jain doctrine. Many technical terms and classifications are only hinted at in the text and require explanation from traditional commentaries and related scriptures. Serious study of Tattvārthasūtra therefore involves reading it alongside authoritative commentaries and, where possible, learning from qualified teachers who can clarify doctrinal nuances and sectarian differences in interpretation.
